(CNN) -- A large ice shelf is "imminently" close to breaking away from part of the Antarctic Peninsula, scientists said Friday. Scientists are investigating whether the ice breakup is caused by global climate change. Satellite images released by the European Space Agency on Friday show new cracks in the Wilkins Ice Shelf where it connects to Charcot Island, a piece of land considered part of the peninsula. The cracks are quickly expanding, the ESA said. Scientists are investigating the causes for the breakups and whether it is linked to global climate change. The Wilkins Ice Shelf -- a large mass of floating ice -- would still be connected to Latady Island, which is also part of the peninsula, and Alexander Island, which is not, said professor David Vaughan, a glaciologist at the British Antarctic Survey. The ice shelf experienced a great amount of changes last year, the ESA said. In February 2008, the shelf dropped 164 square miles (425 square kilometers) of ice. In May it lost a 62-square-mile chunk. That meant the "bridge" of ice connecting Wilkins to the islands was just 984 yards wide at its narrowest location, the ESA said. Further rifts developed in October and November, said Angelika Humbert of the Institute of Geophysics at Germany's Muenster University. "During the last year the ice shelf has lost about 1800 square kilometers (694 square miles), or about 14 percent of its size," Humbert said. Antarctica's ice sheet was formed over thousands of years by accumulated and compacted snow. Along the coast, the ice gradually floats on the sea, forming massive ledges known as ice shelves, the ESA says. Several of these ice shelves, including seven in the past 20 years, have retreated and disintegrated. The Wilkins Ice Shelf had been stable for most of the past century before it began retreating in the 1990s. "It had been there almost unchanged since the first expeditions which mapped it back in the 1930s, so it had a very long period of real stability, and it's only in the last decade that it's started to retreat," Vaughan said. Wilkins is the size of the state of Connecticut, or about half the area of Scotland. It is the largest ice shelf on the Antarctic Peninsula yet to be threatened. If the ice shelf breaks away from the peninsula, it will not cause a rise in sea level because it is already floating, scientists say. Some plants and animals may have to adapt to the collapse. The Antarctic Peninsula is the piece of the continent that stretches toward South America.

A colossal section of ice on the Antarctic Peninsula is poised to break away from the continent, according to glaciologists monitoring a rapidly expanding rift that now stretches more than 100 miles across the Larsen C ice shelf.

The crack, which scientists have tracked with mounting concern over the past several years, has accelerated its advance in recent months, leaving only a narrow band of ice connecting a massive iceberg to the main shelf. When it finally severs, researchers say, it will produce one of the largest icebergs ever recorded—covering an area of roughly 2,000 square miles.

The Larsen C ice shelf is the fourth-largest in Antarctica and the northernmost major shelf on the peninsula, a region that has warmed faster than almost anywhere else on Earth.

"The rift has grown in fits and starts, but the trajectory is clear. It's no longer a question of if, but when."

The break would remove approximately 10 percent of the ice shelf's total area, fundamentally reshaping the peninsula's coastline and potentially destabilizing what remains.

Ice shelves are floating extensions of land-based glaciers. Because they already float on the ocean, their collapse does not directly raise sea levels—much as a melting ice cube does not overflow a glass. But scientists caution that their role is far more consequential than that comparison suggests.

"Ice shelves act like corks in a bottle," explained Dr. Helena Fricker, a glaciologist specializing in Antarctic ice dynamics. "They buttress the glaciers behind them, holding back the flow of ice from the land into the sea. When you remove that buttressing effect, the glaciers can accelerate dramatically."

That acceleration is what worries researchers most. The glaciers feeding into Larsen C hold enough ice to raise global sea levels by about four inches if they were to eventually flow into the ocean.

The concern is grounded in recent history. Larsen C's neighbors to the north, Larsen A and Larsen B, met catastrophic ends in 1995 and 2002, respectively. The Larsen B collapse was particularly stunning—an area comparable to Rhode Island disintegrated in just over a month.

"When Larsen B shattered, it happened with a speed that shocked the scientific community," said Dr. Fricker. "Glaciers that had been stable for centuries suddenly sped up by as much as eightfold. That's the cautionary tale hanging over everything we do here."

Scientists remain careful to distinguish between the two questions at play. Calving—the process by which icebergs break off—is a natural phenomenon that occurs even without human influence.

"We have to be honest about the science," Dr. Luckman noted. "This particular calving event may be part of a natural cycle. What we can't yet say with certainty is whether the loss of this section will trigger a broader retreat, or whether the remaining shelf will stabilize."

Still, he added, the broader context is unmistakable. "The Antarctic Peninsula has warmed by nearly 3 degrees Celsius since the mid-20th century. That's several times the global average. Against that backdrop, the health of these ice shelves is something we ignore at our peril."

## Watching and Waiting

"We monitor it week by week, sometimes day by day," said Dr. Fricker. "Nature will decide the exact moment. Our job is to understand what happens next—and to learn everything we can from it."

Once the iceberg breaks free, scientists will watch closely to see whether the Larsen C shelf finds a new stable configuration or begins the kind of unraveling that claimed its neighbors.

*Understanding the science behind one of Antarctica's most closely watched ice shelves*

## A Shelf Under Stress

The Wilkins Ice Shelf, located on the southwestern side of the Antarctic Peninsula, has become one of the most studied examples of ice shelf instability in the region. Over a series of events beginning in the late 1990s and accelerating between 2008 and 2009, the shelf lost substantial portions of its area, with dramatic breakup events captured by satellite imagery from the European Space Agency and NASA.

At its most precarious point, the remaining shelf was held in place largely by a narrow strip of ice connecting Charcot and Latady Islands—an ice bridge that scientists watched with concern. When that bridge collapsed in April 2009, it removed a critical structural support and raised questions about the stability of the broader ice mass.

## The Climate Connection

The Antarctic Peninsula has warmed significantly over the past several decades—faster than the global average—making it one of the most rapidly changing regions on the planet. This warming is widely attributed to a combination of factors:

- **Rising atmospheric temperatures**, which promote surface melting and the formation of meltwater that can penetrate and weaken ice through a process called hydrofracturing
- **Warmer ocean waters** circulating beneath ice shelves, thinning them from below
- **Shifting wind and circulation patterns** linked to broader climate change

Scientists studying the region, including researchers associated with the British Antarctic Survey and NASA, have connected the pattern of ice shelf retreats along the peninsula—including Larsen A, Larsen B, and Wilkins—to this regional warming trend. While no single collapse event can be attributed to climate change in isolation, the cumulative pattern of ice shelf disintegration is consistent with a warming climate.

## What It Means for Sea Levels—An Important Distinction

Here is a crucial point often misunderstood in public discussion: **the collapse of a floating ice shelf does not directly raise sea levels.**

Because ice shelves are already floating on the ocean, they have already displaced their volume of water—much like ice cubes in a glass. When they break apart, sea level is largely unaffected by that ice itself.

The real concern is **indirect but significant**. Ice shelves act as barriers that hold back the glaciers and ice sheets behind them on land. When shelves collapse, they can allow grounded land ice to flow more quickly toward the ocean. It is *this* land-based ice, once it enters the sea, that contributes to sea level rise.

Studies following the Larsen B collapse demonstrated exactly this effect, with glaciers behind the former shelf accelerating markedly. The Wilkins situation, while somewhat different in its glacial context, reinforced concerns about the "buttressing" role ice shelves play.

## The Bigger Picture

The Wilkins events serve less as a direct sea-level threat and more as a **warning indicator**—a visible sign of how sensitive Antarctic ice systems are to warming. Scientists view these breakups as valuable case studies for understanding processes that may unfold on a larger and more consequential scale, particularly in West Antarctica, where far greater volumes of ice are potentially vulnerable.

The lesson from Wilkins is one of interconnected systems: atmosphere, ocean, floating ice, and grounded ice all influence one another. Monitoring these shelves, researchers say, provides essential early evidence for projecting future changes.

## Conclusion

The retreat of the Wilkins Ice Shelf stands as a striking illustration of Antarctic change in a warming world. While its immediate contribution to sea level rise is minimal, its significance lies in what it reveals about the fragility of polar ice and the importance of the shelves that hold continental ice in check. As monitoring continues, Wilkins remains a reminder that the polar regions are sensitive barometers of our changing climate.

These shelves can range from tens to hundreds of meters thick and span areas comparable to small nations. Crucially, they serve as a braking system for the glaciers behind them. By pressing against coastlines, islands, and the seafloor, ice shelves slow the flow of grounded ice into the ocean.

This distinction is important for sea level: because ice shelves already float, their collapse does not directly raise sea levels—much like a melting ice cube in a full glass does not cause overflow. However, when a shelf disintegrates, the glaciers it once held back can accelerate dramatically, discharging land ice into the sea and contributing to global sea level rise.

## A History of Stability—Until Recently

The Wilkins Ice Shelf had remained largely stable for much of recorded observation. For most of the 20th century, it showed little sign of the dramatic changes now unfolding. Its position on the Antarctic Peninsula, however, placed it in one of the fastest-warming regions on Earth.

Over recent decades, the Antarctic Peninsula has warmed by several degrees Celsius—far outpacing the global average. This warming has been implicated in a cascade of ice shelf collapses along the peninsula. The Larsen A shelf disintegrated in 1995, followed by the spectacular breakup of Larsen B in 2002, which lost an area of roughly 3,250 square kilometers in a matter of weeks. These events reshaped scientists' understanding of how quickly ice shelves can fail.

The Wilkins began showing signs of instability in the late 2000s, when a series of dramatic breakup events removed large sections of ice. Warm air temperatures produce surface meltwater, which can seep into crevasses and wedge them open through a process known as hydrofracturing. Warming ocean waters simultaneously thin shelves from below. Together, these forces have pushed the Wilkins toward the point of collapse.

## What Comes Next

Should the ice bridge fail, researchers anticipate the loss of thousands of square kilometers of ice shelf. While the immediate sea level impact would be minimal, scientists view the Wilkins as a bellwether—a warning of how a warming climate can destabilize even long-stable features of the Antarctic system.

"Each of these collapses tells us something about the sensitivity of the ice to climate change," a polar scientist explained. "The peninsula is giving us a preview of processes that could eventually affect much larger parts of Antarctica."

For now, satellites and monitoring stations remain trained on the thinning ribbon of ice, waiting to document a collapse that many consider not a question of if, but when.
